title: Credit, borrowing costs and protecting your credit score
objective: Calculate the cost of borrowing, compare credit options, and explain the factors that build or damage a credit score.
body:
Credit lets you use money now and repay it later, but it always has a price. Knowing how that price is calculated, and how lenders judge you, separates smart borrowing from expensive debt.

**Types of credit.** **Installment credit** is a fixed amount repaid in equal scheduled payments, such as an auto loan, student loan or mortgage. **Revolving credit**, like a credit card, gives a credit limit you can borrow against, repay and borrow again. A **secured loan** is backed by **collateral** the lender can take if you default, such as the car on an auto loan; an **unsecured loan** has no collateral, so it usually carries a higher rate.

**The cost of borrowing.** The **annual percentage rate (APR)** expresses the yearly cost of credit, including interest and certain fees, so it is the best figure for comparing offers. On a credit card, paying only the **minimum payment** stretches repayment over years and multiplies the interest paid. A **grace period** lets cardholders avoid interest entirely when they pay the full statement balance by the due date. For loans, a longer term lowers the monthly payment but raises total interest. For example, a $20,000 car loan at 7% costs roughly $3,800 in interest over five years, but about $2,300 over three years.

**Credit reports and scores.** A **credit report** records your borrowing and payment history and is kept by the three national bureaus: Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. You can get free reports from each bureau through AnnualCreditReport.com and should dispute any errors you find. A **credit score**, such as a FICO score ranging from 300 to 850, summarizes that report. FICO weighs five factors:
1. Payment history, about 35%
2. Amounts owed, including **credit utilization**, about 30%
3. Length of credit history, about 15%
4. New credit, about 10%
5. Credit mix, about 10%

Credit utilization is your revolving balances divided by your total credit limits. Keeping it under 30%, and lower if possible, helps your score. Late payments, especially those 30 or more days past due, can stay on a report for up to seven years.

**Protecting yourself.** The Fair Credit Reporting Act gives consumers the right to see and dispute their reports, and federal law limits liability for unauthorized credit card charges to $50. A **credit freeze** blocks new accounts from being opened in your name and is free at each bureau. Be wary of payday loans and rent-to-own deals, whose effective APRs can reach several hundred percent.

The most common mistake students make is believing that closing an old, paid-off credit card always helps their score. Closing it removes available credit, which can raise utilization, and it can eventually shorten the average age of accounts, so the score may actually drop.
examples: Sam has $900 of balances across cards with $3,000 in total limits, so his credit utilization is 30%; paying the balances down to $300 drops it to 10%.
A home equity loan is secured by the house, so it usually offers a lower APR than an unsecured personal loan for the same amount.
Rosa pays her full statement balance every month within the grace period, so she uses her credit card without ever paying interest.

questions.stem: Dev has two cards: $400 owed on a $1,000 limit and $200 owed on a $2,000 limit. What is his overall credit utilization?
questions.explanation: Total balances of $600 divided by total limits of $3,000 equals 20%. The 40% figure is only the first card's utilization, not the overall ratio.

questions.stem: Which factor carries the most weight in a FICO credit score?
choices: Payment history
Credit mix
Length of credit history
Number of new accounts opened
questions.explanation: Payment history is about 35% of a FICO score, the largest share. Length of credit history matters, but it is only about 15%.

questions.stem: Kiara is choosing between a 36-month and a 60-month auto loan for the same amount at the same APR. Which statement is true?
choices: The 60-month loan has a higher monthly payment and less total interest
Both loans cost the same total interest because the APR is equal
The 36-month loan has a higher monthly payment but less total interest
The 36-month loan has a lower monthly payment and more total interest
questions.explanation: A shorter term means larger payments but less time for interest to build, so total interest is lower. Equal APRs do not mean equal total cost, because the longer loan charges interest for two more years.

questions.stem: A lender offers Marcus a loan backed by his paid-off pickup truck. What is the truck called in this agreement?
choices: A co-signer
Collateral
A grace period
Revolving credit
questions.explanation: Collateral is property pledged to secure a loan that the lender can claim if the borrower defaults. A co-signer is a person who shares responsibility for the debt, not property.

questions.stem: Nora has paid off a credit card she opened four years ago and wants to close it to 'clean up' her credit. What is the most likely effect?
choices: Her score will definitely rise because she has less debt
Nothing, because closed accounts are removed from reports immediately
Her credit report will be erased and restarted
Her utilization may rise and her score may fall
questions.explanation: Closing the card removes its limit from her available credit, so the same balances on other cards produce a higher utilization ratio. A paid-off card is not debt, so closing it does not reduce what she owes.

questions.stem: When comparing a credit card offer and a personal loan offer, which number best captures the yearly cost of each?
choices: The annual percentage rate (APR)
The minimum payment
The credit limit
The annual percentage yield (APY)
questions.explanation: APR states the yearly cost of borrowing, including interest and some fees, on a standard basis. APY is used for savings returns, not for comparing loans.

questions.stem: After a data breach exposed her Social Security number, Tasha wants to stop anyone from opening new credit in her name. What should she do?
choices: Close all of her existing bank accounts
Request a higher credit limit
Place a credit freeze with each of the three credit bureaus
Pay only the minimum on her credit cards
questions.explanation: A credit freeze blocks lenders from pulling her report, so new accounts cannot be opened in her name, and it is free at each bureau. Closing her bank accounts does not stop fraudsters from opening new credit.

questions.stem: Owen owes $1,500 on a card with a 24% APR and pays only the minimum each month. What is the main consequence?
choices: The balance will be paid off faster than with larger payments
The interest rate will automatically drop
His credit limit will be lowered to the minimum payment
Repayment will take years and total interest will be much higher
questions.explanation: Minimum payments mostly cover interest, so the principal shrinks slowly and total interest grows. Smaller payments can never pay a balance off faster than larger ones.

flashcards.definition: The yearly cost of borrowing, including interest and certain fees, used to compare credit offers.
Revolving credit balances divided by total credit limits; best kept under 30%.
Property pledged to secure a loan that the lender can take if the borrower defaults.
A fixed loan amount repaid in equal scheduled payments, such as an auto loan.
A free block at each credit bureau that prevents new accounts from being opened using your credit report.
